projects.title: Quantum Circuit Causality Engine
projects.short: An open-source tool that works out which gates and qubits actually influence each measurement outcome in a quantum circuit.
projects.description:
Every quantum circuit contains operations that matter to a given measurement and operations that cannot possibly affect it. Telling them apart is currently done by hand, or not at all. This project builds a tool that does it automatically: given a circuit, it constructs the causal dependency graph linking gates, qubits and measurements, and derives the light cone of each measurement outcome — the set of operations that could have reached it.

The same structure explains how errors travel. A fault on a gate outside a measurement's light cone cannot affect that result; a fault inside it has a path, and the graph shows the path. That makes the tool useful for two things at once: understanding what a circuit is really doing, and deciding where error mitigation and optimisation effort is worth spending.

The output is a documented Python package, published openly with its tests and worked examples, so the analysis can be checked and reused rather than taken on trust.
objectives: Build a causal dependency graph from an arbitrary quantum circuit, gate by gate
Derive the backward light cone of every measurement and the forward light cone of every gate
Trace how a fault at any point in the circuit propagates to the measured results
Release the tool as an open-source package with a reproducible test suite
projects.needs: Quantum circuits and algorithms · quantum information theory · software engineering for quantum tools · graph theory and causal analysis · error mitigation and circuit optimisation. You do not need all five. The project needs people who can reason about circuits and people who can build software, and those are rarely the same person.

projects.title: Quantum-Inspired Machine Learning for Disease Prediction
projects.short: A feature-mapping and interpretability study asking whether quantum-inspired kernels help on the small, noisy health datasets African clinical research actually produces.
projects.description:
Quantum-inspired feature maps are nonlinear kernel transforms motivated by parameterised quantum circuits, and they run on ordinary hardware. The open question is whether they classify better than classical kernels on small, noisy data — the situation common in African health research, where a study may have a few hundred labelled cases rather than a few hundred thousand.

Candidate datasets include malaria microscopy, malaria rapid-test metadata and TB screening records. Quantum-inspired kernels are compared directly against classical baselines on the same splits, with the same preprocessing, so the comparison means something.

Accuracy is not the only measure. A model a clinician cannot interrogate is not usable in a clinic, so the study also asks what each approach gives up in interpretability and what it costs to train and run. Both findings get published. A clear negative result is more valuable than a positive one nobody can reproduce.

Data note for the site: any clinical dataset used must be openly licensed or covered by an agreement with the institution holding it, with ethics approval where required. Settled before modelling starts, not after.
objectives: Assemble and document a small set of openly licensed, low-data African health datasets
Implement quantum-inspired feature maps and matched classical baselines under one evaluation protocol
Measure classification performance, interpretability and computational cost side by side
Publish the pipeline and the results, including where the quantum-inspired approach does not help
projects.needs: Quantum machine learning · classical ML and kernel methods · biomedical or clinical data · interpretable and explainable ML · research data governance.

projects.title: Lightweight ML for Predicting Quantum Material Properties
projects.short: Small, interpretable models that predict material properties well enough to tell an experimentalist which candidates are worth making.
projects.description:
New-material discovery is a small-data problem. Open materials databases are large in total but thin in any particular corner, and the groups running the experiments often have neither the compute nor the data volume that large models assume. The question is whether small, interpretable models trained on carefully curated subsets can predict bandgap — or absorption edge — accurately enough to be useful.

"Useful" is defined narrowly and deliberately: not to replace measurement, but to rank candidates so that limited laboratory time goes to the most promising ones first. A model that is roughly right about the ordering is worth more to a lab on a small budget than one that is precisely right but cannot be run or explained.

The output is a reproducible pipeline — curation, feature engineering, model, evaluation — documented so another group can rerun it on their own subset. Throughout, the emphasis is on features a materials scientist recognises rather than a representation only the model understands.
objectives: Curate reproducible subsets of open materials databases for a defined property and material class
Engineer physically meaningful features, and document why each one is there
Train and evaluate small interpretable models against the standard larger baselines
Test whether the ranking is good enough to guide experimental selection, and publish the pipeline end to end
projects.needs: Materials science and condensed-matter physics · DFT and computational chemistry · interpretable ML for small datasets · data curation and reproducible pipelines · experimentalists willing to test the predictions.

projects.title: Feasibility of Satellite Quantum Communication Across Africa
projects.short: Link budgets, key rates and pass windows for satellite QKD between African research hubs — and a first ranked list of city pairs worth a pilot.
projects.description:
Satellite quantum key distribution has been demonstrated elsewhere. Whether, and where, it is viable across Africa is a separate question, and it turns on things a general study does not model: the geography of the continent, its atmospheric conditions, the ground infrastructure that exists at each candidate site, and the hours in which a link is actually available.

This study works that out for a defined set of African research hubs. For each candidate pair it computes the link budget, the achievable secret key rate under realistic loss and background light, and the temporal windows in which a pass is usable — then folds in what is known about the ground infrastructure at each end.

The output is a roadmap rather than a demonstration: maps, link budgets, assumptions stated openly, and a prioritised list of city pairs where a pilot would have the best chance. It is meant to be the document a group takes to a funder or a space agency when proposing one.
objectives: Define candidate ground sites across the continent, and the criteria for including them
Model link budgets and secret key rates for each pair under realistic atmospheric and background conditions
Determine usable pass windows and expected availability across the year
Produce continent-scale maps and a ranked, justified shortlist of pilot city pairs
projects.needs: Quantum communication and QKD · satellite and orbital mechanics · optics and atmospheric propagation · geospatial analysis and cartography · telecommunications infrastructure and policy.

projects.title: Quantum Education LLM for African Communities
projects.short: A domain-specific language model for quantum computing education, built for the contexts, prior backgrounds and constraints African learners actually have.
projects.description:
A general-purpose model can answer a quantum computing question. What it cannot easily do is tell whether the person asking has already met linear algebra, whether they are on a phone with a data cap, or whether the example it just reached for means anything where they live. This project asks what a model built specifically for quantum education across African communities would need to do differently.

Three constraints shape it. Prior background varies enormously, so the model has to meet a learner where they are rather than where a syllabus assumes. Language and context matter, so worked examples should be recognisable. And resources are finite, so it has to remain usable on modest hardware and an intermittent connection.

The project runs alongside the AI Tutor and feeds into it.

[ SCOPE TO CONFIRM WITH THE PROJECT LEAD — whether this is fine-tuning an open model, building a retrieval layer over curated quantum teaching material, or both. ]
objectives: Assemble and license a curated corpus of quantum computing teaching material
Adapt a model to that corpus and to varied prior backgrounds, and evaluate it on real learner questions
Establish what is required to run it under realistic bandwidth and hardware constraints
projects.needs: NLP and LLM fine-tuning · quantum education and curriculum design · retrieval systems and evaluation · multilingual NLP and localisation · teachers and students willing to test what gets built.

projects.title: Quantum Computing for Healthcare Applications
projects.short: Where in the biomedical research pipeline quantum methods could genuinely shorten a computation — and where they could not.
projects.description:
Biomedical research contains several stages that are computationally expensive: molecular simulation, structure and binding prediction, optimisation over large combinatorial spaces. Quantum computing is often proposed for these in general terms. This project takes the narrower and more useful question — which specific stages have a structure a quantum or hybrid method could actually help with, on hardware that exists or is credibly near.

The work is a mapping exercise before it is an implementation one: identify the candidate stages, characterise what makes each one hard, and match them against what these algorithms can currently do. Ruling a stage out is a result, and a more honest one than a demonstration that only works on a toy instance.

[ SCOPE TO CONFIRM WITH THE PROJECT LEAD — which stage or stages the project will take on, and whether the output is a survey, a benchmark or a prototype. ]
objectives: Map the computationally intensive stages of a defined biomedical research pipeline
Match each against quantum and hybrid algorithms, and state the hardware each would require
Benchmark one candidate stage against the classical method it would replace
Publish the assessment, including the stages where a quantum approach is not warranted
projects.needs: Quantum algorithms · computational biology, chemistry or bioinformatics · high-performance and hybrid computing · benchmarking and numerical methods.

projects.title: Secure Quantum Machine Learning
projects.short: Whether quantum machine learning models can be attacked, how, and what it takes to make them trustworthy.
projects.description:
Classical machine learning has a well-developed literature on how models fail under attack: adversarial examples, data poisoning, model extraction, privacy leakage from training data. Quantum machine learning is young enough that the equivalent picture is incomplete. This project asks which of those attacks carry over unchanged, which change shape in a quantum or hybrid pipeline, and which are new.

The security question is inseparable from a trust question. A model whose failure modes are unknown and whose behaviour cannot be audited should not carry a decision that matters — and that holds for a quantum model exactly as it does for a classical one.

[ SCOPE TO CONFIRM WITH THE PROJECT LEAD — which threat model and which class of QML model the project takes on first. ]
objectives: Survey the known attacks on classical ML and assess which transfer to quantum models
Characterise the threat models specific to quantum and hybrid pipelines
Demonstrate at least one attack, and evaluate the defences proposed against it
Publish a threat model and practical recommendations for building QML systems
projects.needs: Quantum machine learning · adversarial ML and AI security · cryptography and security analysis · privacy-preserving machine learning.

legal.privacy:
Quantum Africa (“Quantum Africa”, “we”, “our”, or “us”) respects your privacy and is committed to protecting the personal information of everyone who interacts with our website, programmes, events and community.

This Privacy Policy explains what information we may collect, how we use it, how we protect it, and the choices available to you.

Information We Collect

Depending on how you interact with Quantum Africa, we may collect:

Name and contact information, such as email address.
Country, institution, university or professional affiliation.
Information provided when registering for events, programmes, courses or opportunities.
Information submitted through application, membership or interest forms.
Professional information, such as research interests, skills or LinkedIn profile.
Communications you send to us.
Technical information relating to your use of our website, such as browser, device and basic usage information.
Photographs, videos or other media captured during Quantum Africa activities, where applicable and subject to appropriate notice or consent.

We aim to collect only information that is reasonably necessary for the purpose for which it is collected.

How We Use Your Information

We may use your information to:

Provide and administer Quantum Africa programmes and services.
Register participants for events, courses and workshops.
Communicate with members, participants, partners and applicants.
Send newsletters, announcements and information about relevant opportunities.
Manage chapters, communities and programmes.
Improve our educational resources and digital platforms.
Facilitate research, mentorship and professional opportunities.
Understand participation and measure the impact of our programmes.
Maintain the security and functionality of our website.
Meet legal, regulatory or administrative requirements.

We will not use personal information for purposes that are incompatible with the purpose for which it was collected without an appropriate legal basis or, where required, your consent.

Newsletters and Communications

If you subscribe to a Quantum Africa mailing list, we may use your email address to send newsletters, educational resources, event announcements and relevant opportunities.

You may unsubscribe from non-essential communications at any time using the unsubscribe mechanism included in our emails or by contacting us.

Sharing Information

Quantum Africa does not sell personal information.

We may share information with trusted service providers where necessary to operate our programmes, website, registration systems, communication platforms or other services.

We may also share information where:

You have given permission to do so.
It is necessary to provide a service or opportunity you requested.
It is required by law.
It is necessary to protect the rights, safety or security of Quantum Africa, our community or others.

Where appropriate, we seek to ensure that third parties handling information on our behalf provide reasonable privacy and security protections.

International Transfers

Quantum Africa works across Africa and with international universities, organizations and partners. As a result, information may sometimes be processed or stored in countries other than the country in which you are located.

Where required by applicable law, we will take appropriate measures to protect personal information transferred internationally.

Data Security

We take reasonable technical and organizational measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, loss, misuse, alteration or disclosure.

However, no online system can be guaranteed to be completely secure.

Data Retention

We retain personal information only for as long as reasonably necessary for the purposes for which it was collected, unless a longer retention period is required by law or is necessary for legitimate organizational purposes.

Your Rights

Depending on applicable law, you may have rights concerning your personal information, including the right to:

Request access to information we hold about you.
Request correction of inaccurate information.
Request deletion of your information.
Withdraw consent where processing is based on consent.
Object to certain forms of processing.
Request restriction of processing in certain circumstances.

To exercise a right or ask a privacy-related question, contact us at:

Email: [privacy@quantum-africa.org]

Third-Party Services

Our website and programmes may use third-party services for event registration, email communication, analytics, hosting, educational platforms or other functions. These services may process information according to their own privacy policies.

Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. The latest version will be published on this page with its updated date.

legal.conduct:
Quantum Africa Community Code of Conduct

Quantum Africa is committed to creating an open, respectful, inclusive and scientifically rigorous community where people can learn, collaborate, conduct research and build meaningful relationships.

Our community includes students, researchers, educators, professionals, entrepreneurs, mentors, universities, organizations and partners from across Africa and around the world.

Everyone participating in Quantum Africa activities is expected to contribute to a positive environment.

Respect Everyone

Treat all community members with professionalism, dignity and respect.

We welcome people with different backgrounds, disciplines, levels of experience, perspectives and areas of expertise.

Disagreement is acceptable.

Disrespect is not.

Learn and Collaborate

Quantum Africa is built around collaboration and knowledge sharing.

Members are encouraged to:

Ask questions.
Share knowledge.
Help newcomers.
Give constructive feedback.
Credit the work of others.
Collaborate across disciplines and countries.

We encourage healthy scientific debate while maintaining respect for other participants.

No Harassment

Harassment, intimidation, threats, bullying or unwanted personal attention are not tolerated.

This includes inappropriate behavior during:

Online discussions.
Discord and other community platforms.
Webinars.
Workshops.
Conferences.
University activities.
Meetings.
In-person events.
Private communications connected to Quantum Africa activities.

Professional Communication

Members should communicate professionally when representing Quantum Africa.

Do not use Quantum Africa platforms to:

Promote hate or discrimination.
Threaten or target individuals.
Share sexually explicit or abusive material.
Engage in personal attacks.
Spread malicious or deliberately harmful content.
Impersonate Quantum Africa or another community member.

Scientific Integrity

Quantum Africa promotes responsible and collaborative science.

Members should:

Give appropriate credit to collaborators.
Avoid plagiarism.
Clearly distinguish established results from speculation.
Respect research confidentiality.
Respect intellectual-property rights.
Avoid fabricating or deliberately misrepresenting scientific results.

Confidentiality

Information shared privately within research projects, applications, partnerships or organizational activities should not be disclosed publicly without authorization.

Members participating in specific projects may be required to sign additional confidentiality or intellectual-property agreements.

Representation of Quantum Africa

Only authorized representatives may speak officially on behalf of Quantum Africa or make commitments on behalf of the organization.

Chapter leaders and representatives should follow Quantum Africa's organizational, branding and communication guidelines.

Reporting Concerns

If you experience or witness behavior that violates this Code of Conduct, you are encouraged to report it to Quantum Africa.

Reports should be sent to:

Email: contact@quantum-africa.org

Reports will be handled as confidentially as reasonably possible.

Consequences

Depending on the circumstances, violations may result in:

A warning.
Removal of inappropriate content.
Temporary suspension from community activities.
Removal from an event or programme.
Removal from a chapter or leadership position.
Termination of membership or participation.
Referral to appropriate authorities where required.

Quantum Africa will consider the circumstances and seriousness of each case when determining an appropriate response.

Our Commitment

We want Quantum Africa to be a place where someone can join with curiosity, regardless of their current level of knowledge, and find a community where they can learn, contribute, collaborate and grow.

Respect the community. Share knowledge. Build together.

pages.about.heroLede: Quantum Africa is building the people, knowledge, research capacity, and institutional connections Africa needs to participate in, and help shape, the global quantum future.
pages.about.whoWeAreBody:
Quantum Africa is a pan-African organization advancing quantum science and technology through education, research, talent development, and collaboration. We connect students, researchers, educators, universities, professionals, and partners across Africa and beyond.
Our work is focused on building lasting capacity—not simply delivering individual programmes or events. We create pathways that enable people to learn, develop skills, conduct research, access opportunities, collaborate internationally, and grow into leaders in the quantum ecosystem.
pages.about.storyBody:
Quantum Africa was with a simple conviction: Africa should not be a passive observer of the quantum revolution. The continent has talented students, researchers, and institutions, but greater access to education, research opportunities, networks, and global collaboration is needed to unlock this potential.

The organization began by bringing together students, researchers, and quantum enthusiasts through educational activities, community engagement, and knowledge sharing. What started as an initiative to make quantum computing more accessible gradually grew into a broader pan-African effort focused on developing talent and strengthening the emerging quantum ecosystem.

As the community expanded, Quantum Africa developed national chapters, educational programmes, research initiatives, workshops, webinars, and international collaborations, creating new pathways for African talent to engage with quantum science and technology.

Today, Quantum Africa is building the foundations for a connected continental ecosystem, linking people, universities, research, opportunities, and global partners to help develop Africa’s quantum capacity for the long term.
pages.about.missionBody: To build Africa’s capacity in quantum science and technology by expanding access to quality education, strengthening research and innovation, developing the next generation of quantum leaders and workforce, and connecting African talent and institutions with the global quantum ecosystem.
pages.about.visionBody: An Africa with the knowledge, talent, institutions, and networks to actively shape the global quantum future.
objectivesList: Expand quantum education across African universities and learning communities
Connect African students and researchers with global opportunities
Strengthen MSc and PhD pathways in quantum science and technology
Support collaborative research and develop pan-African research networks
Build partnerships between African and international universities and research institutions
Develop and strengthen Quantum Africa chapters across the continent
Increase African participation and leadership in the global quantum ecosystem.
pages.about.philosophyBody: We believe that access is the first step, but capacity is the goal. Education creates knowledge. Research turns knowledge into expertise. Connection creates opportunities for collaboration and growth. Leadership enables people to shape the future of the field.
